title: The Lake of Fire
hook: If Death itself is thrown into the lake of fire, can it be a torture chamber?
tldr: Revelation's lake of fire draws on the Dead Sea, once called the Lake of Fire, and on the refiner's crucible where sulfur purifies gold. Its torment is testing, its forever means ages of ages, and casting Death and Hades into it shows the death of death: purifying, restorative judgment, not eternal torture.
big_idea: The lake of fire is God's refining crucible, where death itself dies.

points.title: Revelation is symbolic
points.text: Seven-headed dragons, locust-faced creatures and fire-breathing witnesses cannot be literal. The lake of fire should be read as the first readers did: as a metaphor.

points.title: The Dead Sea was the Lake of Fire
points.text: In the First-Temple period the Dead Sea was called the Lake of Fire. It erupted tar, smoke, sulfur and flames, yet its mineral waters still heal and purify.

points.title: Sulfur refines gold
points.text: A limné can be a small pool. Fire and sulfur pictured a refiner's crucible where sulfur draws impurities out of gold. Christ counsels buying gold refined by fire.

points.title: Torment means testing
points.text: Basanizo comes from the touchstone used to test precious metals. Forever and ever is better rendered in the ages of ages, a future period, not eternity.

points.title: Where death dies
points.text: Death and Hades are cast into the lake, so it must be abstract. The second death is the destruction of death, the last enemy, swallowed up in victory.

points.title: No more tears
points.text: God promises no more death, mourning, crying or pain. Only reconciling everyone could end all mourning, so the lake is a crucible purging sin, not a torture chamber.

points.title: Even Satan restored?
points.text: Gregory of Nyssa taught apokatastasis: God's punishments are corrective, so purifying fire would eventually redeem all beings, even the Devil.

sections.summary: Very little in Revelation can be read literally. Almost every element draws on the Hebrew Scriptures, first-century culture and Roman politics. It tells of a red dragon with seven heads, a sea beast with ten horns and seven heads, locusts with human faces, four colorful flying horses, and two witnesses breathing fire on enemies. Read literally, these yield bizarre conclusions. So the lake of fire and sulfur should be read as the original recipients did: as metaphor, not a tangible location.

sections.h: Lake of Fire = The Dead Sea
sections.summary: In the First-Temple period the Dead Sea, or Sea of Salt, was sometimes called the Lake of Fire or Fiery Lake. For thousands of years, up to the first century, it erupted tar, pitch, bitumen, asphaltites, smoke, sulfur and flames, so the Greeks named it Lake Asphaltites. Philo said its valley was full of fires very hard to extinguish, long smoking and burning. The geographer Strabo called it a land of fires, smelling of sulfur and brimstone.

Today people with skin conditions flock from around the world to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on Earth, for its mineral-rich waters, including sulfur, famed for healing and purifying. Bathing in it can feel like dipping in fire, very painful if water gets in your eyes or touches a skin condition or tiny cut, but the healing is worth the pain.

sections.h: A place to cast away sin
sections.summary: Judaism saw the lake as a place to cast away sinful objects: the Talmud says vessels bearing the image of the sun, moon or a dragon should be cast into the salt sea. Like Christian baptism, immersion in the Mikvah is linked with purification from sin, helping a Jew do Teshuva. Water symbolizes cleansing, so the Dead Sea can picture purification by painful baptism, sin left behind in the dead waters.

Revelation 20:10 has the Devil, beast and false prophet in the lake of fire and sulfur, tormented day and night forever and ever, and some translations make it the most terrifying place imaginable. But no ancient Israelite pictured Lake Michigan, about 22,400 sq mi; Israel's largest lake, the Sea of Galilee, is about 64 sq mi. The Greek limné can mean a pond of any size, suggesting a small pool of molten metal in a refiner's crucible, not a vast lava lake holding billions.

sections.h: Sodom's fire and sulfur, and its restoration
sections.summary: For a Jew, fire and sulfur evoke Sodom and Gomorrah, on which the Lord rained sulfur and fire (Genesis 19:24). Yet Ezekiel promises God will bring back the captives of Sodom and her daughters along with Samaria and Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16:53-55). Ezekiel saw the final outcome of God's judgment on Sodom in a very positive light.

Anciently, fire and sulfur symbolized gold refining. Sulfur converts unwanted metals into sulfides that react and smoke, letting purer gold settle in the crucible. Christ tells Laodicea to buy gold refined by fire (Revelation 3:18). Today sulfur makes sulfuric acid for fertilizer, petroleum refining and chemicals; the United States Mint uses it for metal purity. It treated skin infections until the 1940s and serves in insecticides, fungicides and glass. Anciently fire and sulfur were painful but beneficial, not the Middle Ages' symbols of sadistic punishment.

Torment translates the Greek basanizo, originally a touchstone: a black, silicon-based stone for testing precious metals' purity. It means an unpleasant process of testing and refinement, not torture. The Greek behind forever and ever is perhaps better rendered in the ages of ages, a future period of time, not the modern philosophical idea of eternity, which is absent from the Bible.

sections.h: Tormented in the presence of the Lamb
sections.summary: Revelation 14:10-11: worshipers of the beast drink God's wine of fury, are tormented with burning sulfur in the presence of the angels and the Lamb, and the smoke rises forever. Do they suffer only in that presence? Heaven sadistically watching people burn would contradict the restful peace of Revelation 14:13. The angels may symbolize the churches' spirits (Revelation 1:20). Rather, Jesus' presence torments them by confronting their allegiance to the beast, as the two witnesses tormented opponents (Revelation 11:10): inner spiritual anguish.

Smoke rising forever and ever is a vivid metaphor for the finality and completeness of God's judgment: a smoked sacrifice will not stand up and run again. Revelation warns against idolatry and rebellion and stresses God's justice, focusing on the lasting consequences of rejecting God's ways, not perpetual torment in the afterlife.

sections.h: Death and Hades cast in: the second death
sections.summary: Death and Hades are cast into the lake of fire, the second death (Revelation 20:14). Throwing abstract powers into a torture place makes no sense, so the lake too is abstract: God's purifying judgment overcoming death and the grave. Death is the last enemy destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26), swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). The God of Life (Genesis 2:7, Job 33:4, Acts 17:25, John 1:3-4, Psalm 36:9) triumphs. The second death is where death dies.

God is the God of Justice and Lord of Hosts (1 Samuel 1:3), but also rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4) and mighty to save (Zephaniah 3:17). Human kings and generals kill and destroy; the God of Israel also restores and resurrects. Death is not the end: death itself will be cast into the purifying lake of fire and sulfur.

The cowardly, faithless, detestable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their portion in the lake of fire and sulfur, the second death. Death means an end, not an unending ordeal, and fire and sulfur mean purification. These behaviors bring destruction and chaos; the second death eradicates them. Cowards are not tortured forever; sin is defeated, in line with renewal and restoration.

Four verses earlier, God wipes every tear: no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4). Mourning can only end if everyone's memories are erased, Men in Black style, or if everything and everyone is reconciled, which only an omnipotent and omnibenevolent God can do. So the second death is a step in eradicating evil and purifying creation; the lake is a divine crucible purging sin and restoring holiness. God's judgment is restorative, not merely punitive.

Gregory of Nyssa, a saint in Eastern Orthodoxy, Catholicism, Oriental Orthodoxy, Anglicanism and Lutheranism, taught apokatastasis, restoration or reconstitution: all creation, Satan included, finally reconciled to God. Since God is infinitely loving and just, punishment must be corrective, and purifying fire would lead all beings, even the Devil, to repentance. He saw endless, purposeless torture as incompatible with divine justice and love, and judgment fire as purifying, not literal eternal torment.

One may reject Satan's redemption, doubt his existence, dispute hell's role in purification, or question Gregory's Ransom Theory of Atonement, which shaped Christianity for a millennium. Yet his view rests on God being just and also loving, kind, forgiving and gracious even to sinners (Matthew 5:45), creating humanity from overflowing love. For a Jew remembering Hitler's atrocities this is emotionally hard, yet God is far more gracious than we are, and this reflects his character better than eternal torment.

The original audience, familiar with Jewish apocalyptic literature, would hear fire, sulfur, brimstone, smoke and torment (metal testing) as metaphors for purification, corrective judgment and eradicating evil, themes of justice, discipline, restoration and renewal. The lake of fire is a refiner's crucible with sulfur, testing for purity. Wrongdoers may feel the pain they inflicted yet be saved, as one escaping through the flames: where sin increased, grace increased all the more (Romans 5:20).

mythfact.myth: The lake of fire is a vast lava lake holding billions of people.
mythfact.fact: Israel's largest lake is about 64 sq mi, and limné can mean a small pool, like a refiner's crucible.

mythfact.myth: Fire and sulfur always meant sadistic punishment.
mythfact.fact: Anciently they were painful but beneficial: sulfur refined gold, and the Dead Sea's sulfurous waters heal.

mythfact.myth: Forever and ever means endless eternity.
mythfact.fact: The Greek is better rendered in the ages of ages, a future period; the philosophical concept of eternity is absent from the Bible.

mythfact.myth: The second death is never-ending suffering.
mythfact.fact: Death and Hades are cast in; the second death is the destruction of death itself, the last enemy.

quiz.why: It erupted tar, smoke, sulfur and flames, so it was called the Lake of Fire, and by the Greeks Lake Asphaltites.

options: Abstract powers thrown in show the lake is abstract and death is destroyed
It proves Hades is a person
